lessons.title: Hyperkalemia: Stabilize, Shift, Remove
lessons.summary: ECG may be normal despite dangerous potassium; treatment concepts have three distinct goals.

sections.title: 1) Causes
paragraphs: Renal failure, medications, acidosis, cell breakdown/crush, tumor lysis and hypoaldosteronism. Pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis must be considered when context conflicts.

sections.title: 2) ECG
paragraphs: Peaked T waves, PR prolongation, P-wave loss, QRS widening and sine-wave pattern can occur, but ECG sensitivity is limited.

sections.title: 3) Stabilize membrane
paragraphs: IV calcium antagonizes cardiac membrane effects but does not lower serum potassium. It is used for significant ECG toxicity/peri-arrest according to protocol.

sections.title: 4) Shift vs remove
paragraphs: Insulin/glucose and beta-agonist shift K intracellularly; bicarbonate has selected roles. Definitive removal requires renal/GI strategies or dialysis depending on situation.

lessons.title: Hyponatremia: Brain Swelling, Symptoms & Safe Correction
lessons.summary: severity depends on symptoms, acuity and tonicity—not sodium number alone.

sections.title: 1) Neurologic danger
paragraphs: Acute hypotonic hyponatremia can cause cerebral edema → headache, vomiting, confusion, seizure and coma. Chronic adaptation reduces edema risk but increases risk from overly rapid correction.

sections.title: 2) Initial questions
paragraphs: Is it true hypotonic hyponatremia? Acute or chronic? Seizure/coma? Volume status? Medications, polydipsia, SIADH, heart/liver/kidney disease?

sections.title: 3) Severe symptoms
paragraphs: Hypertonic saline bolus strategies are used for severe neurologic symptoms under protocol with close sodium monitoring.

sections.title: 4) Overcorrection hazard
paragraphs: Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia can cause osmotic demyelination; hospital management requires controlled targets and frequent labs.

lessons.title: Acute Kidney Injury: Perfusion, Toxins & Obstruction
lessons.summary: AKI is a syndrome with pre-renal, intrinsic and post-renal mechanisms; emergencies often arise from complications.

sections.title: 1) Mechanisms
paragraphs: Pre-renal: low perfusion. Intrinsic: tubular/glomerular/interstitial injury. Post-renal: obstruction. Mixed etiologies are common in sepsis/critical illness.

sections.title: 2) Immediate threats
paragraphs: Hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, severe acidosis and uremic complications can be life-threatening.

sections.title: 3) Assessment
paragraphs: Trend urine output, creatinine if available, volume status, medication/toxin exposure, sepsis, obstruction symptoms and ECG.

sections.title: 4) Avoid harm
paragraphs: Review nephrotoxins and avoid reflex large fluid loads when pulmonary edema/heart failure is present.

lessons.title: Dialysis Patient Emergencies: Hyperkalemia, Volume, Access & Missed Dialysis
lessons.summary: dialysis patients can deteriorate from electrolyte, volume and access-related problems.

sections.title: 1) Missed dialysis
paragraphs: Hyperkalemia, acidosis, uremia and pulmonary edema are major consequences. Ask last dialysis and residual urine output.

sections.title: 2) Access
paragraphs: AV fistula/graft hemorrhage can be catastrophic; use direct pressure/hemostatic measures and protect access. Avoid routine BP/IV use in fistula arm when alternatives exist per local practice.

sections.title: 3) Hypotension after dialysis
paragraphs: Consider excessive ultrafiltration but also sepsis, bleeding, cardiac ischemia and arrhythmia.

sections.title: 4) ECG
paragraphs: Treat suspected hyperkalemic cardiotoxicity promptly according to protocol rather than waiting for lab confirmation when the clinical picture is compelling.
